Benjamin Britten. The English composer from 1913 to 1976, he was the preeminent voice of twentieth-century British music, revitalizing British opera and choral music. A pacifist who left England for the United States during the early years of World War II, his works often center on themes of the social outsider, innocence corrupted, and the tragedy of war. His breakthrough opera Peter Grimes in 1945 put English opera back on the international map. He is widely celebrated for his educational work The Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra and his monumental War Requiem.

Peter Grimes is his tragic opera about a misanthropic fisherman in a small Suffolk village who faces social ostracism after his apprentices die at sea. It is famous for the atmospheric orchestral Four Sea Interludes. The Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra is a popular educational piece based on a theme by Baroque composer Henry Purcell. It systematically introduces each section of the orchestra before concluding with a grand fugue. War Requiem was composed for the consecration of the rebuilt Coventry Cathedral, destroyed by German bombs. It combines the Latin Mass for the Dead with the anti-war poetry of Wilfred Owen. Peter Pears was the tenor singer, muse, and lifelong partner of Britten, for whom he wrote the title role of Peter Grimes and many other leading vocal parts. Billy Budd is Britten's all-male opera from 1951 based on Herman Melville's sea novella, set aboard the HMS Indomitable during the French Revolutionary Wars. The Aldeburgh Festival is the music festival Britten co-founded in 1948 in the Suffolk coastal town where he lived and worked.

Britten stands as a key English voice of twentieth-century classical music. He authored Peter Grimes and Billy Budd, two of the most significant English-language operas. He adapted major works by Herman Melville, Henry James through The Turn of the Screw, and William Shakespeare through A Midsummer Night's Dream.
